body.en: Finding a maximum or minimum of \( f(x,y) \) starts the same way it did in single-variable calculus — at a smooth extremum, the derivative vanishes. The difference is that now "the derivative" is a vector, and once it vanishes, you need a second test to tell a peak from a valley from a saddle. That test turns out to be a \( 2\times2 \) determinant, straight out of Linear Algebra Chapter 4.

\( (a,b) \) is a critical point of \( f \) if \( \nabla f(a,b)=\mathbf{0} \) — that is, \( f_x(a,b)=f_y(a,b)=0 \) — or if a partial derivative fails to exist there. Every local max or min where \( f \) is differentiable occurs at a critical point (if some direction had \( D_{\mathbf{u}}f\neq0 \), moving that way would increase or decrease \( f \), so the point couldn't be extremal).

At a point where the second partials exist, the Hessian matrix is \[ H=\begin{pmatrix}f_{xx}&f_{xy}\\f_{yx}&f_{yy}\end{pmatrix}, \] and (using \( f_{xy}=f_{yx} \) from Clairaut's theorem) its discriminant is \[ D=\det(H)=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2. \]
The sign of \( D \), together with the sign of \( f_{xx} \), classifies every non-degenerate critical point.

Let \( (a,b) \) be a critical point of \( f \), with \( f \)'s second partials continuous near \( (a,b) \), and let \( D=D(a,b) \) as in Definition 3.2.

  • If \( D>0 \) and \( f_{xx}(a,b)>0 \): \( f \) has a local minimum at \( (a,b) \).
  • If \( D>0 \) and \( f_{xx}(a,b)<0 \): \( f \) has a local maximum at \( (a,b) \).
  • If \( D<0 \): \( (a,b) \) is a saddle point (neither a local max nor min).
  • If \( D=0 \): the test is inconclusive.

Write \( h,k \) for small displacements and drop the argument \( (a,b) \) from \( f_{xx},f_{xy},f_{yy} \). Since \( (a,b) \) is critical, the first-order terms of \( f \)'s Taylor expansion vanish, and — provided \( D eq0 \) — the quadratic term dominates the remainder for \( (h,k) \) small, so the sign of \( f(a+h,b+k)-f(a,b) \) matches the sign of the quadratic form \[ Q(h,k)=f_{xx}h^2+2f_{xy}hk+f_{yy}k^2. \]

Case \( f_{xx} eq0 \). Completing the square in \( h \): \[ Q(h,k)=f_{xx}\Big(h+ rac{f_{xy}}{f_{xx}}k\Big)^{2}+\Big(f_{yy}- rac{f_{xy}^2}{f_{xx}}\Big)k^2=f_{xx}\Big(h+ rac{f_{xy}}{f_{xx}}k\Big)^{2}+ rac{D}{f_{xx}}k^2, \] using \( f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2/f_{xx}=(f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2)/f_{xx}=D/f_{xx} \).

If \( D>0 \) and \( f_{xx}>0 \), both \( f_{xx} \) and \( D/f_{xx} \) are positive, so \( Q(h,k) \) is a sum of two nonnegative terms, zero only when both squared terms vanish — which (since \( D/f_{xx} eq0 \)) forces \( k=0 \), then \( h=0 \). So \( Q(h,k)>0 \) for every \( (h,k) eq(0,0) \): a local minimum. If \( D>0 \) and \( f_{xx}<0 \), both coefficients are negative by the same reasoning, so \( Q(h,k)<0 \) away from the origin: a local maximum. If \( D<0 \), then \( f_{xx} \) and \( D/f_{xx} \) have opposite signs: along \( k=0 \), \( Q=f_{xx}h^2 \) has the sign of \( f_{xx} \); along \( h=-(f_{xy}/f_{xx})k \), \( Q=(D/f_{xx})k^2 \) has the opposite sign. \( Q \) takes both signs arbitrarily close to \( (0,0) \): a saddle point.

Case \( f_{xx}=0 \). Then \( D=-f_{xy}^2\le0 \) automatically, so only the \( D\le0 \) rows of the theorem are reachable here, and only \( D<0 \) (i.e. \( f_{xy} eq0 \)) is claimed. Here \( Q(h,k)=2f_{xy}hk+f_{yy}k^2 \). Taking \( (h,k)=(1,\varepsilon) \) for small \( \varepsilon eq0 \) gives \( Q\approx2f_{xy}\varepsilon \), whose sign flips with the sign of \( \varepsilon \); so \( Q \) again takes both signs arbitrarily close to the origin — a saddle point, matching the theorem.

Classify the critical points of \( f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2 \).

\( f_x=3x^2-3=0\Rightarrow x=\pm1 \); \( f_y=2y=0\Rightarrow y=0 \). Critical points: \( (1,0) \) and \( (-1,0) \).

\( f_{xx}=6x \), \( f_{yy}=2 \), \( f_{xy}=0 \), so \( D=12x \).

At \( (1,0) \): \( D=12>0 \) and \( f_{xx}=6>0 \) — local minimum, value \( f(1,0)=1-3=-2 \).

At \( (-1,0) \): \( D=-12<0 \) — saddle point.

The second derivative test optimizes \( f \) freely over the whole plane. Often, though, you need the best value of \( f \) only among points satisfying some constraint \( g(x,y)=c \) — walking along a fixed curve rather than roaming the plane.

Suppose \( f \) has a local extremum, subject to the constraint \( g(x,y)=c \), at a point \( (a,b) \) where \( abla g(a,b) eq\mathbf{0} \). Then there exists a scalar \( \lambda \) with \[ abla f(a,b)=\lambda\, abla g(a,b). \]

Since \( abla g(a,b) eq\mathbf{0} \), the level curve \( g(x,y)=c \) has a smooth parametrization \( \mathbf{r}(t)=(x(t),y(t)) \) near \( (a,b) \), with \( \mathbf{r}(t_0)=(a,b) \) and \( \mathbf{r}'(t_0) eq\mathbf{0} \) tangent to the curve.

Because \( g(\mathbf{r}(t))=c \) is constant along this curve, the chain rule (Definition 2.1) gives \( abla g(a,b)\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t_0)=0 \): the gradient \( abla g(a,b) \) is orthogonal to \( \mathbf{r}'(t_0) \).

Since \( (a,b) \) is a local extremum of \( f \) restricted to the constraint, \( h(t)=f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \) has a local extremum at \( t=t_0 \), so \( h'(t_0)=0 \). By the chain rule again, \( h'(t_0)= abla f(a,b)\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t_0)=0 \): the gradient \( abla f(a,b) \) is also orthogonal to \( \mathbf{r}'(t_0) \).

So both \( abla f(a,b) \) and \( abla g(a,b) \) are orthogonal to the same nonzero vector \( \mathbf{r}'(t_0) \) in \( \mathbb{R}^2 \). In the plane, the set of vectors orthogonal to a given nonzero vector is a single line through the origin (a 1-dimensional subspace) — so any two vectors orthogonal to \( \mathbf{r}'(t_0) \) are scalar multiples of each other. Hence \( abla f(a,b)=\lambda\, abla g(a,b) \) for some scalar \( \lambda \) (taking \( \lambda=0 \) if \( abla f(a,b)=\mathbf{0} \)).

label.en: Worked example 3.B — Using a Lagrange multiplier

body.en:
Maximize \( f(x,y)=xy \) subject to \( x+y=10 \).

Here \( g(x,y)=x+y \), so \( abla g=(1,1) \) — never \( \mathbf{0} \), so Theorem 3.2 applies at any extremum. \( abla f=(y,x) \). Setting \( abla f=\lambda abla g \): \[ y=\lambda,\qquad x=\lambda\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] Combined with \( x+y=10 \): \( x=y=5 \), so \( f(5,5)=25 \) is the constrained maximum (checking nearby constrained points, e.g. \( (9,1) \) gives \( f=9 \) and \( (6,4) \) gives \( f=24 \), both less than \( 25 \), consistent with a maximum here).
